516: (9) A kli rishon — meaning the vessel that was used on the fire — cooks even after it has been removed from the fire, as long as the hand is scalded in it. Therefore it is forbidden to place spices in it, or even salted meat; but bull's meat [meaning meat that is hard to cook] is permitted. And salted meat — because of the blood in it — is forbidden. And one who puts salt in a kli rishon — even though it was removed from the fire — a blessing comes upon him if he did not violate a prohibition. {Rama: And the more stringent one is praiseworthy. And one who places salted meat in it when it is on the fire — even if not salted — is also forbidden.}
519: (12) 'Even after it has been removed, etc.' — the Beit Yosef wrote in the name of the Hagahot Mordechai that it is closest to say that it is only called a kli rishon from the moment it is removed from the fire, but if one left it to cool even in a place where the hand is scalded in it, it loses its status as a kli rishon.
521: (13) 'Salted meat' — the Rosh wrote that it implies bull's meat is not cooked in a kli rishon and it is permitted to place raw meat in a kli rishon that was removed from the fire. However if it is old salt it causes cooking.
523: (14) 'And some forbid placing salt' — in the Gemara there are two versions. According to the second version, salt is treated leniently since it is hard to cook like bull's meat — therefore it is permitted even in a kli rishon. According to the first version it is treated stringently since it requires cooking — therefore it is forbidden even in a kli sheni.
525: (15) 'Nullified on top of the food' — and it is not a davar she'yesh lo matirin after Shabbos, since even in a thousand it would not be nullified. But here it is nullified before the prohibition takes effect, since salt does not cook except in a kli rishon, and it is nullified before it cooks.
527: (28) 'As long as it is yad soledes bo' — and it appears to me that if it is not yad soledes bo it is permitted, even though for the matter of forbidden and permitted there are those who forbid, as written in Toras Chatas klal 57 — that is because it absorbs and expels.
529: (29) 'Of bull' — the fact that the meat does not cook — the moisture within it cooks (Tur).
531: (30) 'Blood in it' — and we are dealing with meat that was rinsed after salting, otherwise it is still forbidden because of the blood in it. And the clear intent of the Beit Yosef implies specifically when it is still salted does placing it in a kli rishon render the blood forbidden.
533: (31) 'The salt is nullified in sixty' — and even though something that imparts flavor is not nullified — here it is different for it is zeh v'zeh gorem, since it was already salted before Shabbos as well. And even though a davar she'yesh lo matirin is not nullified, since this applies after Shabbos it is nullified before the prohibition.
535: (24) 'Scalded' — see the Magen Avraham and see Yoreh De'ah siman 94 note 2 what is written there in the name of the Maharshal.
537: (25) 'Of bull' — the fact that the meat does not cook — the moisture within it cooks. Tur.
539: (26) 'Blood' — and we are dealing with meat that was rinsed after salting, otherwise it is still forbidden because of the blood in the salt. And the clear intent of the Beit Yosef implies specifically when it is still salted the blood becomes forbidden.
541: (27) 'Salt' — I have already written in note 17 that the same applies to onions since they are sharp and cook quickly, and we observe that when placed in a hot kli sheni they become visibly soft.
543: (28) 'Nullified' — see the Taz who disagrees and concluded that this eating should not be permitted on Shabbos but one should wait until after Shabbos — see there, and see the Magen Avraham.
545: (27) 'Seif 9 is forbidden according to all' — meaning even according to the first view, and all this is according to the Rosh and Shulchan Aruch seif 4. But according to the Maggid Mishneh cited in seif 15 in the gloss.
547: (28) 'As long as the hand is scalded in it' — if it is not yad soledes bo, there is no concern of cooking. This is why throughout this siman it states 'the hand is scalded,' and even a kli rishon that is not yad soledes bo is considered like a kli sheni.
549: (29) 'Since they removed it' — Rashi there s.v. dib'chli.
551: (30) 'And there is' — the Rosh there, and see the Taz in the name of the Rosh; the Tur did not mention salted meat.
553: (31) 'And some forbid' — like the first version.
555: (32) 'And those who are stringent' — Tosafos there.
557: (33) 'Even he, etc.' — on the fire even according to the ruling of the Shulchan Aruch it is forbidden as stated above.
559: (34) 'The salt' — see the Magen Avraham. And what is written regarding something that imparts flavor — see in Chullin 97b and in Avodah Zarah 69a. And what is written regarding zeh v'zeh gorem — see in Pesachim 26-27.
561: (5) 'Nullified' — see the Beer Heitev and the Peri Megadim, siman 84: those who bring hot water in a kli rishon on Shabbos that is fully boiled — if one erred and poured from the kli rishon into small bowls that have ground spices in them, if the bowls are kli sheni the spices are not forbidden.
563: (59) 'All the time, etc.' — meaning even after it has stopped boiling.
565: (60) 'The hand is scalded in it' — but if the hand is not scalded in it, even a kli rishon does not cook. And if it was not removed from the fire it is forbidden to place spices in it.
567: (61) 'To place spices in it' — but in a kli sheni it is permitted to place spices even when yad soledes bo, since they do not cook there. And if a solid item is placed in a kli sheni that is yad soledes bo there are grounds for stringency.
569: (62) 'Since they removed it' — on the fire, even bull's meat cooks.
571: (63) 'Like bull's meat' — and even though it melts even in a kli sheni, its melting is not its cooking, for even in cold you see the same thing.
573: (64) 'Salted meat' — meaning meat that was salted and rinsed according to the law.
575: (65) 'Of bull' — the fact that the meat does not cook — the moisture within it cooks [Tur].
577: (66) 'Without salting, etc.' — we were not led to think that the reason it is forbidden is because the salt softens the meat and it then cooks in a kli rishon. Rather even without being salted the moisture within it cooks.
579: (67) 'And some forbid, etc.' — in the Gemara there are two versions: according to the second version, salt is treated leniently since it is hard to cook like bull's meat — therefore it is permitted even in a kli rishon. According to the first version it needs cooking — therefore it is forbidden even in a kli sheni.
581: (68) 'Even he, etc.' — on the fire even according to the ruling of the Shulchan Aruch it is forbidden, as above.
583: (69) 'The salt is nullified' — even though something that imparts flavor is not nullified, here it is different for it is zeh v'zeh gorem — here we are dealing with meat that was already salted before Shabbos as well, and the salt was already absorbed into the meat.
585: (60) 'The hand is scalded in it' — the reality is that most things do not cook when placed in a kli rishon that is removed from the fire. But there are things that do cook in it, and these are enumerated in this seif.
587: (61) 'Spices' — even spices (and not like salt mentioned in the continuation of the sentence). And in seif 10 it appears that it is forbidden even to pour from a kli rishon onto spices.
589: (62) 'Like bull's meat' — meaning: salt requires cooking like beef. That is: salt certainly does not cook in a pot removed from the fire, and therefore it is permitted to add salt to it.
591: (63) 'Of bull' — according to this view, since the salt somewhat softens the meat, the meat may cook slightly even in a kli rishon that is not on the fire.
593: (64) 'Also forbidden' — according to the Rama, the stringent view forbids placing bull's meat in a kli rishon that is on the fire even without salt, for the decree against a kli rishon on the fire is general.
595: (65) 'Because of the blood in it' — even meat that was salted and the blood removed is forbidden to place in a kli rishon, because it cooks it on Shabbos; but meat that was not salted is forbidden to place in it because of the blood.
597: (66) 'That it is yad soledes bo' — according to this view one should be concerned that salt cooks easily.
599: (67) 'May a blessing come upon him' — from the primary law it is permitted to give salt in a vessel that is not on the fire even when it is hot, and as halacha one may rely on this. However there is room to be stringent.
601: (68) 'Who transgressed a prohibition' — who transgressed the prohibition of cooking by Torah law.
603: (69) 'On top of the food' — even though food cooked on Shabbos is forbidden to eat, as we saw at the beginning of the siman, here the food itself is already cooked and can be eaten even without the added salt. Therefore cooking the salt does not retroactively render the food itself forbidden.
606: 'And if he passed and gave salt, etc.' — and regarding spices, when placed in a kli rishon even though a small amount was also given before Shabbos, one should examine b'dieved regarding the dish, for it is a davar she'yesh lo matirin. But Rabbeinu Simcha permits salt since it dissolves immediately and does not cook, for salt requires cooking etc. And it is nullified before it becomes forbidden. But regarding spices this is not so, and it is possible that here too it is nullified before it cooks — and this requires further study.
